result:
I have always liked the idea that ordinary days can contain hidden doors if you pay enough attention. The world rarely announces its mysteries; instead, it offers tiny clues and trusts curious people to notice. A scratched coin, a song played twice, or the particular silence of a friend can become an invitation. Most of us walk past such invitations because responsibility has taught us to value schedules over wonder.

For years, I kept a notebook filled with questions that seemed too small to deserve answers. Why do some streets feel welcoming while others make you hurry? Why does bread smell like home before anyone has even opened the bakery door? Why do old books sometimes open to pages that perfectly match the mood of the day? I did not know what the notebook would become, only that emptiness felt less honest than curiosity.

Then, one autumn evening, I met an elderly woman at a railway station with a paper bag full of lemons. She said she collected lemons wherever she traveled, though she had never explained why. Her hands were stained yellow, and a map in her pocket was covered with circles. When I asked about the map, she smiled and said, “Every circle is a place where I remembered being happy.” That sentence changed the way I saw my own notebook.

Now, whenever something catches my attention, I write it down instead of pretending it is unimportant. Some entries are profound; most are silly. And that is wonderful.
